beats.text: This is me last Friday paying for a lobster I never even tasted. I ordered a burger and a glass of water.
Because somebody at the table said five little words. Let's just split it evenly.
And that friendly little sentence is costing me about fourteen hundred dollars a year.
By the end of this video you'll know the one sentence that got my money back and somehow made my friends like me more.
But most people click away before that part which is exactly why everyone keeps paying for the lobster.
So it starts on a Friday night. I just cut my phone bill and my friends want to celebrate my new rich life.
They pick a steakhouse where the waiter tells you his name. And you know that's never a cheap sign.
I'm being careful this month. So I order the burger and a glass of tap water. Very responsible. Very boring.
Then my buddy Trevor orders the lobster and a cocktail. And then one more cocktail. For safety.
Bob gets the biggest steak on the menu. And somebody orders wine for the whole table without asking anybody.
Me watching the table order while I sip my free water.
Two hours later the bill lands in the middle of the table like a tiny leather bomb.
Four hundred seventy four dollars. And Trevor says it. Let's just split it evenly.
So everybody owes seventy nine dollars. Including me. My burger and my water were twenty one.
And be honest. You know exactly what I did next because you've done it too. I smiled. And I tapped my card.
Me paying for Trevor's lobster with a smile on my face.
I just paid fifty eight dollars for food that went into other people. Mostly into Trevor.
And the worst part? I didn't even get dessert. Trevor got dessert. I paid for a third of a chocolate cake I watched from across the table.
So at home I open my banking app and scroll back through a whole year of dinners with these guys.
We go out twice a month. That's twenty four dinners a year. And I'm always the burger guy.
Fifty eight dollars times twenty four. My calculator says almost fourteen hundred dollars.
That's a real vacation. A beach. A hotel. And I gave it away one lobster claw at a time.
My vacation fund every time someone says let's split it.
But here's the thing. My friends aren't bad people. So why is the bill always so big? Turns out somebody already ran the experiment.
An economist named Uri Gneezy invited students to lunch at a popular restaurant near a big university in Israel.
Every table had six strangers. And each table got a secret rule. Some tables paid for their own food. Some tables split the bill evenly.
Quick guess before I tell you. How much more did the split tables spend? Lock in your number in the comments.
There was even a table where lunch was free. And those people ate more than double. Which won't shock anyone who's ever stood near an open bar.
Me at any event with free food.
But the split tables are the weird ones. Those people paid real money. So why did they order more?
So I grab a napkin and work it out with Trevor's lobster. Forty eight dollars.
If Trevor pays for his own food that lobster costs him forty eight dollars. And he probably orders the chicken.
But split six ways? That same lobster costs Trevor eight dollars. And his friends get the other forty.
So a split bill is a secret coupon. Five sixths off anything you order. And your friends pay for the coupon.
Trevor discovering the split bill coupon.
Economists even have a name for it. The unscrupulous diner's dilemma. It was described in Scientific American back in nineteen ninety four.
And the answer to your guess. The split tables spent about a third more per person. Same food. Same restaurant. Just a different rule.
So the villain isn't Trevor. The villain is the rule. It pays everyone to order more and then it sends the bill to whoever ordered the least.
And guess who loves that rule. The restaurant. It just sold a third more food without printing a single coupon.
The restaurant when six friends ask for one bill.
But then I read one more line of that study. Before lunch they asked people how they wanted to pay.
About eight out of ten said separate bills. Eight out of ten. Almost everybody wanted to pay for their own food.
So think about your last group dinner. Most of your friends were probably sitting there hating the split too. Six people thinking the same thing. And all six smiled and said sure.
Six adults with jobs and bills and opinions. All too scared to say four words to a waiter.
Six friends at the table all secretly hating the split.
Why does nobody say it? Because we'd rather lose fifty eight dollars than look cheap for five seconds.
And dinner is just the small version. That same week the group chat lights up. Trevor turns thirty and he wants a birthday weekend in Las Vegas.
Six hundred forty dollars each. And four thumbs up pop into the chat in under a minute.
Me staring at the group chat with my thumb above the button.
And then there's the wedding. And the bachelor party for the wedding. And the trip for the bachelor party for the wedding.
Here's the wild part. My friends don't just split my bills. They quietly decide what feels normal to me.
Economists studied lottery winners in Canada. And then they watched the neighbors.
When one house on a tiny street won big the neighbors started going bankrupt more often. Not the winner. The neighbors.
Because the winner buys a new car. And then the guy next door needs a new car too. With money he doesn't have.
It's not about the car. It's about not feeling like the poor guy on the street.
The neighbors when one guy wins the lottery.
This is so old it has its own name. In nineteen thirteen a cartoonist started a comic strip called Keeping Up with the Joneses.
And it was based on his own life. He and his wife were living way beyond their money trying to keep up with the neighbors.
Over a hundred years later it's worse. Because now the Joneses live in your phone. You see every trip and every dinner every single day.
In one survey almost a third of Americans said they feel pressure to keep up with how their friends spend. For people my age it's even more.
So I look at the chat. Then at my bank balance. And I type I'm in. Las Vegas goes on my credit card.
Me in Vegas acting rich on a credit card.
Now the damage is over two thousand dollars. I'm going broke so that nobody thinks I'm broke.
So I try a sneaky fix. I show up late to skip the appetizers. And I still pay for the appetizers.
Then I try hiding. I say I'm busy three weekends in a row and I eat cereal over the sink.
I even muted the group chat. Then I watched their Instagram stories alone on my couch eating cereal. Peak loneliness.
Me telling my friends I'm busy this weekend.
That saves money. But it costs me my friends. And the friends were the whole point.
So I'm stuck. Keep my friends and lose my money. Or keep my money and lose my friends.
Then I find a study about the exact thing I'm scared of. Saying no to a friend.
A professor named Julian Givi asked people a simple question. About three out of four admitted they'd said yes to plans they didn't want. Just because they were scared to say no.
Then he tested what really happens. Pick one before I tell you. Did the friends who got a no feel hurt? Or did they barely care?
The people saying no expected a disaster. Angry friend. Hurt friend. Never invited again.
But the friends barely cared. They mostly thought about your reasons. Not about the no.
Me realizing the awkward moment only exists in my head.
So I've been paying fourteen hundred dollars a year to dodge a feeling nobody else is even having.
So here's what I did. Quick reminder this is education and not advice. Three moves.
Move one. Timing. You say it before anybody orders. After the food comes it sounds like an accusation.
Move two. The sentence. No apology. No speech about money. Just this.
Hey I'm doing separate checks tonight. I'm on a budget this month.
Notice what's missing. I never mention the lobster. I never ask anybody else to change anything.
Move three is for the big stuff. Like Vegas or the bachelor trip. I stop saying no. I offer a cheaper yes.
I can't do Vegas but I'll host the birthday cookout and the first round is on me.
Me hosting the cookout instead of flying to Vegas.
And the split math? An app does it now. The story goes that Venmo started because one of two college roommates forgot his wallet.
So Friday comes around again. Same steakhouse. Same waiter. Same five friends.
My heart is pounding like I'm about to rob the place. The waiter walks over. And I just say it.
Separate checks tonight. I'm on a budget.
One full second of silence. Then Bob puts down his menu and says oh thank goodness. Me too.
Then two more friends say the same. Half the table has been dreading that bill for years.
And Trevor stares at the menu for a very long time. And he orders the chicken tenders.
Trevor only loves lobster when it costs eight dollars.
I pay twenty one dollars. Same table. Same friends. Nobody left the group chat. And I get about fourteen hundred dollars a year back.
Two weeks later Trevor texts me. Hey can you send me that budget app you use? Trevor. The lobster guy.
To be fair splitting evenly is totally fine when you all ordered about the same. Or when it's your turn to treat.
It only gets expensive when it's automatic. You can split a lot of things with your friends. You don't have to split a lobster.
Your friends aren't making you broke. The silence is. And the silence ends with one sentence.
Next time I'm dragging my suitcase through the airport and a very smiley man offers me a free flight. All I have to do is sign up for a credit card. What could go wrong?
Subscribe. It's free. And I promise I'll never split the bill with you.
